title: Work that runs without you
desc: What a Cowork task is, how one sentence becomes one, why it waits for your approval, and where its result lands.
learningGoal: After this lesson you can describe the full life of a Cowork task, from the sentence you type to the result that reports back, and say which jobs belong in Cowork rather than in chat.

steps.title: Ask it here, or have it done for you
steps.bodyMd:
At Van Dijk Groep, buyer Bart starts every morning the same way: he opens a chat and retypes the same request, *what came in from suppliers overnight, and what needs an answer today?*

Bee Flow has two halves for that.

- **Chat** answers you here, while you wait. You are present, so you can ask a follow-up.
- **Cowork** does recurring work for you while you do something else: on a schedule, or when something happens, and it reports back.

The page asks it plainly: **What should be done for you?** Each job you hand over becomes a **task**.

We follow one task the whole way: Bart's sentence, the card that checks it, the steps he approves, and the result waiting for him at 07:30.

steps.title: Cowork lives under New Chat
steps.body: The badge on this row counts your tasks that are switched on; a paused task is not counted. Open it and you land on the Cowork home: one column with the box at the top, then what needs you, then your tasks.

steps.title: One sentence, then Show what I understood
steps.body: Type what should happen, and when, in this box. The button reads Show what I understood: it only reads your sentence and shows you what Cowork made of it. Nothing is created yet. Start from a template, beside it, begins from work your organisation already set up.

steps.title: Four lines answer your sentence
steps.bodyMd:
Bart types: *"Every weekday at 07:30, summarise the new supplier mail in Outlook per supplier, with the order number, the amount and the reply deadline, and send it to me."* He chooses **Show what I understood**.

A card headed **This is what I understood** answers with four lines, and every line can be changed right there:

- **What**: the task's name, worked out of the sentence.
- **When**: the day and the time it heard, here every weekday at 07:30.
- **Uses**: the apps his sentence names, as chips. Outlook is one of his apps and the sentence names it, so Outlook is there.
- **Sends to**: **Me**, and any e-mail address written in the sentence.

The same four questions come back on every task, so remember them: What, When, Uses, Sends to.

steps.question: Bart reads the card, sees that When says every weekday at 07:30, and closes his laptop for the day without pressing anything else. What will happen tomorrow at 07:30?

choices.label: Nothing. Show what I understood only read his sentence; no task exists until he presses Set up and test.
The digest runs at 07:30, because the card already shows the right day and time.
choices.feedback: The card is a question, not a task. Reading the sentence creates nothing; only Set up and test (or Start) makes the task.

choices.label: It is saved as a draft under Your tasks, and runs once he opens Cowork again.
choices.feedback: There are no drafts. If the card was never confirmed, there is no row under Your tasks either.

steps.explanation: Reading the sentence and making the task are two separate presses. The card lets you see and correct what Cowork understood before anything exists.

steps.title: Set up and test: fixed steps, tried once
steps.bodyMd:
Bart presses **Set up and test**. Now the task exists, and the home shows three lines ticking past:

1. **Setting up the steps**: Cowork turns his sentence into fixed steps, the same on every run, with AI only where something has to be written or judged.
2. **Testing once, nothing is sent**: the steps run on his real mail, but change and send nothing.
3. **Ready for your check**.

Then a card appears under **Needs you**: *The steps are ready and tested. Check them once.* with **Open and approve**.

Until he approves, the task does not run for real. Not at 07:30, and not by hand either.

(In an organisation without fixed steps the button reads **Start** instead, and the AI works the task out on every run.)

steps.title: The first approval shows what the test produced
steps.bodyMd:
**Open and approve** opens the task as a page. Above its steps sits **This is what you would have received**: the actual text the test produced, from his real data, and who it would have gone to. Nothing was sent.

Bart reads it the way he would read tomorrow's digest. Then he chooses:

- **Approve**: *Approved. It runs by itself from now on.*
- **Change something**: opens the task's **What** so he can say it differently first.

That is the deal Cowork makes with you: you see a real result before it ever runs for real.

steps.question: Saskia in HR pressed Set up and test on Friday for a report every Monday at 08:00, then went home without opening Needs you. It is Monday 09:00. What has happened?

choices.label: Nothing ran. The task still waits for her approval, its status reads Needs you, and its next moment simply moved on.
It ran at 08:00 with the AI working it out, because nobody approved the steps in time.
choices.feedback: Cowork never switches a task to the AI by itself. Only Saskia can choose Let the AI work it out every run; until she chooses, the task waits.

choices.label: It ran with the tested steps, since the test had already passed.
choices.feedback: A passed test is not an approval. The steps run for real only after she presses Approve.

steps.explanation: A task created through the confirmation card is held until its steps are approved. A repeating one skips its moments; nothing is sent in the meantime.

steps.title: Chat, or a Cowork task?
steps.instruction: Four jobs from Van Dijk Groep. Match each one to where it belongs.

pairs.left: Bart needs our payment terms with one specific supplier right now, and may want to dig further.
pairs.note: You are present and you want a conversation. A Cowork run never asks you a question back about what you meant, so anything that needs a follow-up belongs in chat.

pairs.left: A one-off comparison of three steel-frame suppliers, ready to read after this afternoon's site visit.
pairs.right: A task that runs once, today
pairs.note: Real work, no repeat. If the sentence does not say when, the card asks Which day? and Just once, today is the first choice.

pairs.left: Every working day at 07:30, a digest of the new supplier mail with order number, amount and deadline.
pairs.right: A task that runs every weekday
pairs.note: Monday to Friday, whether or not Bart opens Bee Flow. The card's When line shows the day and the time.

pairs.left: Saskia's short progress report on the first of every month, from last month's meeting notes.
pairs.right: A task that runs every month
pairs.note: Same shape, slower drum. She says it in her sentence; afterwards the task's When can be set to Every month too.

steps.title: The home: what needs you comes first
steps.bodyMd:
Under the box the home lists, top to bottom:

- **Needs you**: one card per thing that waits for you. Steps to approve, a message to look at before it goes out, a failure. A failure is always in plain words with one action.
- **Your tasks**: one row per task, with one status word.
- **Shared with you**: tasks colleagues shared with you, only when there are any.
- **Teamwork**: tasks of different people that hand work to each other.

The status word is always one of eight: **Done**, **Failed**, **Needs you**, **Scheduled**, **Running**, **Testing**, **Paused** or **Nothing to do**.

steps.question: Bart's digest has run every weekday for a month. This Tuesday its row reads Nothing to do. What does that tell him?

choices.label: The run went fine and found nothing to do this time, for example no new supplier mail.
It failed quietly and he should look for the error.
choices.feedback: A failure is never quiet: the row would read Failed and a card under Needs you would say what went wrong, with one action to fix it.

choices.label: It is paused until he approves something.
choices.feedback: Those have their own words: Paused when he switched it off, Needs you when it waits for him.

steps.explanation: Nothing to do is a success with nothing to report. Only chase it if you expected output every time; then the sentence or the time is what needs changing.

steps.title: A task opens as a page

steps.question: Saskia's monthly progress report touches personnel data. Who else at Van Dijk Groep can open that task and read its runs?

choices.label: Nobody, unless she shares it herself with a named colleague under Share; even then only she can change it.
Everyone in the organisation: Your tasks is a workspace list, like a shared calendar.
choices.feedback: Your tasks lists only your own. A colleague sees a task only under Shared with you, after its owner shared it.

choices.label: Her colleagues can see it, but only after it has run for a month.
choices.feedback: Time never shares anything. Sharing is a choice the owner makes under Share, per colleague.

steps.explanation: A task belongs to the person who made it and runs as them. Share lets a colleague see it (Can see) or also answer what it asks (Can answer); nobody else can edit it.

steps.title: Your turn: walk the life of one task
steps.instruction: Pick one job you would genuinely hand over, yours or Bart's supplier digest. In four to six sentences, walk it from beginning to end: the sentence you type, what the card's four lines would say, what happens when you press Set up and test, what you check before you approve, and where you read the result once it has run. Write it for a colleague who has never opened Cowork.
steps.placeholder: e.g. I type "Every Friday at 16:00, list this week's quotes that have had no reply, with customer, amount and days of silence, and send it to me." The card would say: What, Open quotes; When, every Friday at 16:00…

steps.title: What you can do now
steps.bodyMd:
- **Tell the two halves apart.** If you want the answer in front of you and may ask a follow-up, chat. If the work should happen while you are elsewhere, make it a Cowork task.
- **Predict what your sentence becomes.** Show what I understood answers with What, When, Uses and Sends to, and nothing exists until you press Set up and test.
- **Know why it waits, and where to read it.** It runs for real only after you approved what the test produced; afterwards the task page, its History and your notifications hold every result.

Next chapter: writing the one sentence so the four lines come out right the first time.

ex-cowork-basics-life.title: The life of a Cowork task
ex-cowork-basics-life.task: The learner picks one job to hand to Cowork and describes it end to end in four to six sentences: the sentence they type, what the confirmation card's four lines (What, When, Uses, Sends to) would say, what Set up and test does, what they check before approving, and where the result is read afterwards.
criteria: Names a concrete job with a timing (once, a day and time, or a repeat) rather than a vague wish.
Describes the card's lines, or at least When and Sends to, and shows that nothing exists until Set up and test (or Start) is pressed.
Says that the steps are set up and tested once without sending anything, and that the task only runs for real after they approve what the test produced.
Says where the result is read: the task page or its History, or the notifications; not in an open chat window or a colleague's screen.
ex-cowork-basics-life.guidance: Pass a plain, specific walkthrough even if the wording is informal. Do not pass an answer that only says "it runs automatically", that skips the approval and claims the task runs straight after it is created, that describes a back-and-forth conversation, or that sends the result to colleagues without naming them under Sends to. Using the old words (Run, Schedule, chips) instead of Show what I understood and Set up and test should fail the second criterion but need not sink the whole answer.

practiceTopic.title: Cowork basics
practiceTopic.summary: How one sentence becomes a Cowork task, why it waits for your approval, how the home and a task page are laid out, and who can see a task.
facts: The Cowork row sits directly under New Chat in the sidebar, and its badge counts the tasks that are switched on.
Show what I understood reads the sentence and answers with a card headed 'This is what I understood' with four lines, What, When, Uses and Sends to; it creates nothing.

Set up and test creates the task, sets up fixed steps and tests them once on real data while sending nothing; where the organisation has no fixed steps the button reads Start and the AI works the task out on every run.
A task created through the card does not run for real until its steps are approved; the first approval shows 'This is what you would have received' with Approve and Change something.
The home lists Needs you, Your tasks, Shared with you (when not empty) and Teamwork; a failure is always a card under Needs you.
Every task has one status word: Done, Failed, Needs you, Scheduled, Running, Testing, Paused or Nothing to do; Nothing to do is a run that found nothing to do, not a failure.
A task opens as a page with Run for real now, Pause and Share at the top, then Settings with the rows What, When, Uses and Sends to, then Steps, People and History.
A task belongs to its owner; colleagues see it only when the owner shares it (Can see or Can answer), and only the owner can change it.
